items.stem: Which term describes the biological differences between males and females, such as chromosomes and reproductive organs?
items.answer: Sex
items.markingKey: Sex: the biological differences between males and females, such as chromosomes and reproductive organs. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “hegemonic masculinity”? Give one example.
items.answer: The dominant, most valued form of masculinity in a society, associated with toughness, heterosexuality and power. Example: a culture celebrating physically strong, competitive men.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the dominant, most valued form of masculinity in a society, associated with toughness, heterosexuality and power); 1 mark for a relevant example such as a culture celebrating physically strong, competitive men. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “gender role socialisation” and “crisis of masculinity”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Gender role socialisation: the process of learning the behaviour and attitudes expected of one’s gender (e.g. boys being told “big boys don’t cry”). Crisis of masculinity: the idea that men are uncertain about their identity because traditional male roles such as breadwinner have declined (e.g. unemployed former industrial workers losing their sense of purpose).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Ethan, a father in Kathmandu, takes six months of parental leave while his partner returns to work, and some of his friends joke that he is “not a real man”. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: identities are fluid, fragmented and chosen; globalisation, the media and consumption allow people to construct hybrid, pick-and-mix identities rather than having them fixed by class, gender or ethnicity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: After the closure of the steelworks near Cairo, many young men say they feel “useless” and spend time in gangs. Explain how a postmodernist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Postmodernism: identities are fluid, fragmented and chosen; globalisation, the media and consumption allow people to construct hybrid, pick-and-mix identities rather than having them fixed by class, gender or ethnicity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Omar, a father in Istanbul, takes six months of parental leave while his partner returns to work, and some of his friends joke that he is “not a real man”. Compare how postmodernist and functionalist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Postmodernism: identities are fluid, fragmented and chosen; globalisation, the media and consumption allow people to construct hybrid, pick-and-mix identities rather than having them fixed by class, gender or ethnicity. Functionalism: identities based on shared roles help integrate individuals into society; socialisation prepares people for roles linked to gender, age and occupation, which contributes to social stability.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Assess how useful official statistics are for studying changes in gender roles over the last forty years.
items.answer: Strengths: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified; they are usually free and readily available, saving time and money. Limitations: they are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs; they show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying changes in gender roles over the last forty years but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: A sociologist in Cape Town wants to research changes in gender roles over the last forty years. Evaluate the use of self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; they are standardised, so the study can be repeated by another researcher to check reliability. Limitations: response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative; closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying changes in gender roles over the last forty years but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “cultural defence”? Give one example.
items.answer: The strengthening of ethnic identity and tradition as a response to hostility or racism from the wider society. Example: a minority group emphasising its religion after experiencing discrimination.

items.stem: Explain the difference between “ethnicity” and “ethnic identity”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Ethnicity: a shared cultural identity based on factors such as language, religion, history, traditions and sense of common origin (e.g. a community sharing a language and religious festivals). Ethnic identity: a person’s sense of belonging to an ethnic group and the meaning they give to it (e.g. a young person identifying strongly as Tamil).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of semi-structured interviews for studying the experiences of minority ethnic young people in schools.
items.answer: Strengths: the interviewer can adapt questions sensitively while still covering the key issues; a core set of questions allows some comparison between interviewees while follow-up questions add depth. Limitations: samples are usually fairly small, so representativeness is limited; interviewer bias may still affect answers. Theory: semi-structured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative and quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the experiences of minority ethnic young people in schools but best combined with another method such as field experiments (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “youth”? Give one example.

items.stem: Explain the difference between “youth” and “childhood”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Youth: the life stage between childhood and adulthood, often associated with independence, peer groups and youth culture (e.g. teenagers developing distinctive fashion and music tastes). Childhood: a stage of life seen in many modern societies as separate from adulthood and requiring protection (e.g. laws banning child labour and making schooling compulsory).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: In one village near Riyadh, children of eight help in the fields and look after younger siblings; in the city itself, children of the same age are not allowed to walk to school alone. Explain how a radical feminist sociologist might interpret this situation.

items.stem: Assess how useful personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) are for studying changes in the way childhood has been represented in the past.
items.answer: Strengths: they allow sociologists to study families and communities in the past that cannot be observed now; they may be the only source of evidence about the past. Limitations: they are usually unrepresentative because only some people keep or publish them; their meaning must be interpreted by the researcher, which may introduce bias. Theory: personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying changes in the way childhood has been represented in the past but best combined with another method such as laboratory experiments (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Study the data, which come from a study of perceptions of when adulthood begins (800 adults, Toronto). Table: percentage agreeing that “a person is an adult by the age of 21” | 1995 | 2025. People aged 18-29 | 50% | 43%. People aged 30-59 | 56% | 47%. People aged 60+ | 55% | 54%. (a) Suppose 300 of the respondents were People aged 18-29. Using the 2025 figure, calculate how many of them gave this response. (b) Explain one reason why these data may not give a valid picture of perceptions of when adulthood begins. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that the boundaries between age stages are becoming blurred.
items.answer: (a) 43% of 300 = 43 ÷ 100 × 300 = 129 (to the nearest whole person). (b) They measure what people say they do, not what they actually do. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure fell for People aged 18-29, People aged 30-59, People aged 60+; People aged 60+ had the highest figure for 2025. The transition to adulthood is now gradual and individualised rather than marked by clear rites of passage. Qualifications: Legal ages for voting, marriage and work still mark clear boundaries; views vary between age groups; experiences differ by class and country. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 800 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark method (43 ÷ 100 × 300); 1 mark answer 129. [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Distinguish between “social mobility” and “embourgeoisement”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Social mobility: movement of individuals or groups between social classes (e.g. the child of a factory worker becoming a lawyer). Embourgeoisement: the idea that affluent manual workers adopt middle-class lifestyles and values (e.g. well-paid factory workers buying their own homes).

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using unstructured interviews to research changes in class identity in a former industrial town.
items.answer: Strengths: they allow people to explain the meanings they give to their experiences in their own words; rapport between interviewer and interviewee builds trust, so people may reveal more, producing valid data. Limitations: they are time-consuming and the data is hard to analyse and compare; the interviewer may lead the interviewee or interpret answers selectively (interviewer bias). Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying changes in class identity in a former industrial town but best combined with another method such as longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Distinguish between “class identity” and “social mobility”, using an example of each.

items.stem: The table shows results from research into attitudes to gender roles, using self-completion questionnaires with 300 adults in Mumbai. Table: percentage agreeing that “a man’s job is to earn money; a woman’s job is to look after the home” | 2000 | 2025. Men | 45% | 29%. Women | 36% | 17%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Women between 2000 and 2025. Show your working. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that traditional gender identities have declined.
items.answer: (a) (17 − 36) ÷ 36 × 100 = -52.8%. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure fell for Men, Women; Men had the highest figure for 2025. The social construction of gender has changed as more women enter paid work. Qualifications: A significant minority still hold traditional views; attitudes may change faster than behaviour (women still do more domestic work); social desirability may lead people to under-report traditional views. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 300 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (17 − 36) ÷ 36 × 100; 1 mark for -52.8% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful participant observation is for studying the experiences of minority ethnic young people in schools.
items.answer: Strengths: it reveals the meanings and labels that shape interaction as it happens; it is flexible and can uncover issues the researcher had not anticipated. Limitations: the observer’s presence may change the group’s behaviour (the Hawthorne effect), especially if overt; studies are small-scale and impossible to repeat exactly, so findings are unreliable and hard to generalise. Theory: participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the experiences of minority ethnic young people in schools but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. items.stem: A research team is investigating experiences of ageism among older workers. Explain two strengths of using covert participant observation for this research.
items.answer: 1. It can give access to closed or deviant groups who would refuse an overt researcher. 2. Because the group does not know it is being studied, members act naturally and the Hawthorne effect is avoided.

items.stem: Arjun is planning a study of experiences of ageism among older workers. Evaluate the use of field experiments for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they take place in a natural setting, so behaviour is more realistic than in a laboratory; participants usually do not know they are part of an experiment, so they act naturally. Limitations: deceiving people about sensitive matters may cause harm or distress; the researcher has much less control over variables than in a laboratory. Theory: field experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying experiences of ageism among older workers but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). items.stem: The table shows results from research into class identity, using self-completion questionnaires with 600 adults in Madrid. Table: percentage describing themselves as | 1990 | 2025. Working class | 50% | 36%. Middle class | 33% | 33%. No class / don’t know | 17% | 31%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Working class between 1990 and 2025. Show your working. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that social class is no longer important to people’s identity.
items.answer: (a) (36 − 50) ÷ 50 × 100 = -28%. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for No class / don’t know; the figure fell for Working class; Working class had the highest figure for 2025. items.answer: Mac an Ghaill’s study found working-class boys who expected manual jobs that no longer existed responded with “macho” behaviour. Criticism: Critics argue the crisis is exaggerated and that masculinities have always been changing.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Interactionism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: After the closure of the steelworks near Santiago, many young men say they feel “useless” and spend time in gangs. Suggest how an interactionist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Interactionism: identity is created and negotiated in interaction; people respond to labels and manage the impressions they give, so identities are active and changeable (Goffman, Mead).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Priya, a sociology student, found the following figures in a report on attitudes to gender roles in Bangkok. The report was based on 600 adults. Table: percentage agreeing that “a man’s job is to earn money; a woman’s job is to look after the home” | 2000 | 2025. Men | 35% | 25%. Women | 25% | 5%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Women change between 2000 and 2025?
items.answer: -20 percentage points
items.markingKey: 5 − 25 = -20 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of self-completion questionnaires for studying representations of femininity on social media.
items.answer: Strengths: there is no interviewer present, so interviewer bias is avoided and anonymity is easier to guarantee; they are standardised, so the study can be repeated by another researcher to check reliability. Limitations: pre-set answers cannot capture the subjective meanings people attach to their experiences; response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying representations of femininity on social media but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes an identity formed by combining elements from two or more cultures?
items.answer: Hybrid identity
items.markingKey: Hybrid identity: an identity formed by combining elements from two or more cultures. [1]

items.stem: Outline what Hall meant by arguing that identities in the modern world are increasingly hybrid and constantly changing.
items.answer: Stuart Hall argued ethnic identities are not fixed essences but are produced through history, culture and representation, and that globalisation creates new hybrid identities.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the idea; 1 mark for developing it: Stuart Hall argued ethnic identities are not fixed essences but are produced through history, culture and representation, and that globalisation creates new hybrid identities. [2]

items.stem: A food festival in Kuala Lumpur serves “fusion” dishes that combine recipes from several migrant communities. Suggest how a Marxist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Marxism: identities are shaped by class position under capitalism; other identities (such as consumer or national identity) may distract people from class inequality and exploitation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: After a rise in racist attacks in Kathmandu, young people from a minority community begin attending their place of worship more often and wearing traditional dress. Explain how a postmodernist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Postmodernism: identities are fluid, fragmented and chosen; globalisation, the media and consumption allow people to construct hybrid, pick-and-mix identities rather than having them fixed by class, gender or ethnicity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of laboratory experiments for studying how second-generation migrants in Madrid see their identity.
items.answer: Strengths: results are quantitative and easy to compare; the researcher controls variables, so cause and effect relationships can be identified. Limitations: it would be unethical to recreate harmful situations, such as violence, in a laboratory; many social issues cannot be studied in a laboratory for ethical or practical reasons. Theory: laboratory experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how second-generation migrants in Madrid see their identity but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes a stage of life seen in many modern societies as separate from adulthood and requiring protection?
items.answer: Childhood
items.markingKey: Childhood: a stage of life seen in many modern societies as separate from adulthood and requiring protection. [1]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which old age is socially constructed.
items.answer: Retirement age and pensions are set by the state; the status of the elderly differs between cultures (respected elders vs. burden); media stereotypes; consumer culture and the “third age”.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained way. [4]

items.stem: A 12-year-old in Madrid has a smartphone, follows adult celebrities online and wears clothes similar to those of her older sister. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: identities are fluid, fragmented and chosen; globalisation, the media and consumption allow people to construct hybrid, pick-and-mix identities rather than having them fixed by class, gender or ethnicity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A 12-year-old in Bangkok has a smartphone, follows adult celebrities online and wears clothes similar to those of her older sister. Explain how a radical feminist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Radical feminism: identities are shaped by patriarchy: gender identities are socially constructed in ways that keep women subordinate to men.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Priya, a sociology student, found the following figures in a report on perceptions of when adulthood begins in Seoul. The report was based on 600 adults. Table: percentage agreeing that “a person is an adult by the age of 21” | 1995 | 2025. People aged 18-29 | 50% | 38%. People aged 30-59 | 58% | 52%. People aged 60+ | 56% | 50%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for People aged 60+ between 1995 and 2025. Show your working. (b) Explain one reason why these data may not give a valid picture of perceptions of when adulthood begins. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that the boundaries between age stages are becoming blurred.
items.answer: (a) (50 − 56) ÷ 56 × 100 = -10.7%. (b) Respondents may misunderstand questions, or give socially desirable answers, and there is no chance to clarify. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure fell for People aged 18-29, People aged 30-59, People aged 60+; People aged 30-59 had the highest figure for 2025. Longer education and later home-leaving have extended youth. Qualifications: Legal ages for voting, marriage and work still mark clear boundaries; views vary between age groups; experiences differ by class and country. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 600 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (50 − 56) ÷ 56 × 100; 1 mark for -10.7% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: State one way in which social class continues to affect people’s life chances.
items.answer: Wealth and income inequality.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. wealth and income inequality. [1]

items.stem: Explain two reasons why class identity may have weakened in many societies.
items.answer: Decline of manual industry and traditional working-class communities; rise of consumer culture and lifestyle-based identity (Pakulski and Waters); increased social mobility and growth of the middle class; other identities (gender, ethnicity, sexuality) have become more important.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained reason. [4]

items.stem: A survey of 400 adults in Lagos produced the data below. Table: percentage describing themselves as | 1990 | 2025. Working class | 57% | 46%. Middle class | 34% | 41%. No class / don’t know | 9% | 13%. By how many percentage points did the figure for No class / don’t know change between 1990 and 2025?
items.answer: +4 percentage points
items.markingKey: 13 − 9 = +4 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using laboratory experiments to research how first-generation university students experience class.
items.answer: Strengths: the procedure is standardised, so the experiment can be repeated to check reliability; results are quantitative and easy to compare. Limitations: it would be unethical to recreate harmful situations, such as violence, in a laboratory; it is impossible to control all the variables that affect human behaviour. Theory: laboratory experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how first-generation university students experience class but best combined with another method such as personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]
